claim: INVEST criteria (Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimatable, Small, Testable) introduced by Bill Wake as a framework for evaluating user story quality
quote: Good user stories are: Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimatable, Small, and Testable

claim: INVEST is a set of guidelines that helps teams evaluate user story quality; stories are an invitation to conversation, not fixed contracts
quote: Stories are an invitation to a conversation. The details evolve through team discussion until reaching a balanced solution between value, cost, and complexity.

claim: Acceptance criteria define conditions a product must meet to be accepted; primary formats are Given/When/Then, rule-oriented checklists, and custom plain-text
quote: Acceptance criteria are 'conditions a software product must meet to be accepted by a user, a customer, or other systems.'

claim: A story with more than 6 acceptance criteria is typically an epic and should be split; rules-based format suits payment-failure and integration boundary cases
quote: Clear, specific conditions that must be met for a user story or feature to be considered complete.

claim: Given/When/Then format is best used during backlog grooming before development; quantify outcomes (< 200 ms) rather than vague qualifiers (fast)
quote: Replace vague language ('fast') with metrics ('response < 200 ms'). Keep it concise: use simple language and focus on one behavior per scenario.

claim: Three AC templates: bullet list (simple flows), scenario-based GWT (complex branching), and checklist (high-stakes multi-team work)
quote: Features with clear boundaries, teams with shared context, straightforward requirements without complex branching logic — use the bullet list.

claim: Nine story-splitting patterns: workflow steps, CRUD operations, business rule variations, data variations, data entry methods, major effort, simple/complex, defer performance, spike
quote: Publishing a news story splits into direct publication, adding editor review, legal review, staging preview, and production deployment.

claim: Story splitting decision: validate it is a user story, identify complexity source (workflows, rules, roles, interfaces, data), then validate split against INVEST
quote: an online checkout feature can be divided into separate stories for adding products to the cart, entering a shipping address, selecting a payment method, and confirming the order.

claim: Three Amigos brings together business (PO), development, and testing perspectives to examine a story before development begins
quote: Three amigos refers to the primary perspectives to examine an increment of work before, during, and after development.

claim: Definition of Ready is the team's agreement on how complete a user story must be before it can be pulled into sprint planning
quote: Definition of Ready (DoR) allows you to evaluate work before your team starts on it. It defines a task, user story, or story point for your team.

claim: Acceptance criteria must be measurable and testable — 'loads in < 2 seconds' not 'loads quickly'; BDD way connects AC to automated test scenarios
quote: If you can't answer 'yes' or 'no' to whether a criterion is met, it's too vague.

claim: Acceptance criteria should be defined before development starts and involve stakeholders with diverse perspectives for shared understanding
quote: Involve stakeholders and team members with diverse perspectives. Make AC clear, concise, and understandable.

claim: Common user story anti-patterns include system-as-actor, epic-as-story, vague acceptance criteria, and implementation-focused acceptance criteria
quote: Stories may be too vague and incomplete — not specifying which platforms or what should happen after login.

claim: INVEST criteria improve communication between PO and dev team and ensure stories are valuable, estimable, and testable before sprint commitment
quote: Well-written INVEST user stories help reduce ambiguity, improve collaboration between product owners and development teams, and ensure that every sprint delivers meaningful value.
